slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
In Bordeaux's 700-year wine history, extreme vintages have been both catastrophes and turning points. The devastating frost of 1956 destroyed vast numbers of old vines overnight, yet also drove industry modernisation; the heatwave of 2003 overturned conventional climate thinking and accelerated innovation in response to climate change; the spring frost of 2017 reduced yields by 40%, yet the surviving grapes produced wines of astonishing quality.

This course systematically analyses the key extreme vintages in Bordeaux's history and provides an in-depth understanding of the characteristics and impact of six major climate risks: spring frost, hail, drought, heatwave, flooding, and disease. We explore how top estates respond to risk through technical defences, insurance mechanisms, and vintage management strategies, and examine how climate change is altering the frequency and intensity of extreme events and the challenges facing the industry.

Course Learning Objectives

📚 Systematic Analysis of Historic Extreme Vintages

Gain an in-depth understanding of the causes, impacts, and industry responses of 10 important extreme vintages including 1956, 1991, 2003, and 2017

⚠️ Understand 6 Major Climate Risk Types

Master the mechanisms, damage patterns, and control methods for spring frost, hail, drought, heatwave, flooding, and disease

🛡️ Master Risk Management Strategies

Learn the five major strategic dimensions: technical defence (fans, candles, anti-hail nets), insurance mechanisms, and vineyard diversification

🍷 Learn Tasting Skills for Extreme Vintages

Understand how extreme climate conditions affect wine style and the principles for evaluating the investment value of extreme vintages

🌡️ Look Ahead to New Challenges under Climate Change

Analyse how global warming is changing the frequency of extreme events and the application of new technologies in climate risk management

On completing this course, you will have a comprehensive understanding of how Bordeaux survives and develops in extreme climates, and what lessons these historical experiences offer for the future.

Estimated study time: 50 minutes

Difficulty level: Advanced Professional
slides.1.title: Historical Records of Bordeaux's Extreme Vintages
slides.1.subtitle: Ten Key Vintages from Which the Industry Learned
slides.2.title: Extreme Vintages: Definition and Three Types
slides.2.content:
⛈️
A vintage in which climate events deviate significantly from the norm, causing yield, quality, or economic losses of a significant level — both a disaster and an opportunity for industry evolution.
⚠️ Catastrophic
Catastrophic Year
Yield loss > 50%
Quality severely damaged; winemaking potential greatly reduced
Examples: 1956 · 1991 · 2017 · 2021
🌡️ Challenging
Challenging Year
Style deviates markedly from the norm
Extreme climate can produce distinctive styles; polarising assessments
Examples: 2003 · 2011 · 2019 · 2022
💎 Opportunity
Opportunity Year
The best stand out in adversity
Producers with meticulous management achieve remarkable quality under difficult conditions
Examples: 2013 · 2018 · 2020
slides.3.title: 10 Extreme Vintages That Changed Bordeaux
slides.3.content:
❄️ 1956
Catastrophic
The Century Freeze
-20°C to -24°C, February
80–90% of vines killed by frost; centuries-old trunks split; thousands of small growers bankrupt.
Legacy: Merlot dramatically increased; Malbec virtually disappeared
❄️ 1991
Catastrophic
Spring Frost Disaster
-3°C to -7°C, 20–21 April
80–90% of new shoots destroyed by frost; yields fell 70–80%; one of the lowest since WWII.
Legacy: large-scale investment in frost protection; insurance sector developed
🌡️ 2003
Challenging
Extreme Heatwave Year
Temperatures exceeded 40°C repeatedly in August
Alcohol 14–15.5%, very low acidity; polarising market reception (a climate wake-up call).
Legacy: redefined 'ripeness' — not just sugar levels
❄️🌫️ 2017
Catastrophic
Spring Frost + Downy Mildew Double Disaster
Losses exceeded €1 billion; 50–70% of buds frost-damaged
Warming caused early bud-break, yet frost still came — a counterintuitive warning of increased vulnerability.
Legacy: warming ≠ end of frost; early bud-break actually increases risk
⚠️ 2021
Catastrophic
Spring Frost + Hail + Downy Mildew Triple Threat
Yields down 25–30%; some appellations –50%+
Consecutive disasters in 2017 and 2021 revealed the systemic issue of rising climate risk frequency.
Legacy: successive disasters → heightened awareness of systemic risk
🔥 2022
Challenging
Hottest and Driest Summer on Record
100+ days above 30°C; almost no rain June–August
Old vines/clay won; young vines/sand lost — clear evidence of Bordeaux shifting towards a Mediterranean climate.
Legacy: irrigation may become a necessity — policy debate intensifies
📌 Spring frost and heatwave/drought are the primary extreme risks, and their frequency is increasing — from 'once in a century' to 'every few years'
slides.4.title: Knowledge Check: Extreme Vintages
slides.4.question: Both 1956 and 2003 were extreme vintages, but their mechanisms of impact were entirely different. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
slides.4.options.0: 1956 was a yield disaster with little quality impact; 2003 was a quality disaster with normal yields
slides.4.options.1: 1956 changed Bordeaux's grape variety composition; 2003 prompted the industry to redefine the concept of 'ripeness'
slides.4.options.2: 1956 mainly affected the Left Bank; 2003 mainly affected the Right Bank
slides.4.options.3: Both prompted large-scale investment in irrigation systems
slides.4.explanation: The Great Frost of 1956 killed 80–90% of vines. When replanting, estates dramatically increased the proportion of the more cold-tolerant Merlot and reduced Malbec (which virtually disappeared), fundamentally changing Bordeaux's variety composition. The extreme heatwave of 2003 caused grapes to ripen extremely early, driving alcohol up to 14–15% and producing overripe flavours that challenged the traditional view of 'late harvest = high quality'. It prompted the industry to develop new systems for assessing ripeness, focusing not just on sugar levels but on phenolic maturity and acid balance. Both were watershed events for the industry.
slides.5.title: In-depth Analysis of Six Major Climate Risk Types
slides.5.subtitle: Understanding the Nature of Threats and Response Strategies
slides.6.title: Climate Risks (Part 1): High-Frequency Core Threats
slides.6.content:
❄️ Spring Frost
Very High
Spring Frost
⏰ Early April – mid-May (bud-break period)
Radiation frost: on calm, clear nights, cold air settles in low-lying frost pockets. –2°C sustained for >2 hours causes serious damage.
  • New shoots blacken and wither
  • Secondary bud-break produces low yields
  • Low-lying plots completely destroyed
🛡 Heaters/fans/sprinklers · late pruning · avoid frost pockets
⚠️ Warmer winters cause earlier bud-break → increased risk of vulnerable period overlapping with frost period
🧊 Hail
Localised Devastation
Hail
⏰ May–August (esp. June–July)
Severe convection forms 1–5 cm hailstones; path unpredictable (hundreds of metres to kilometres wide).
  • Berry skin wounds → entry points for pathogens
  • Single-parcel loss 50–100%
  • Entire vintage destroyed in minutes
🛡 Anti-hail nets · insurance 70–80% coverage · geographic diversification
🌡️ Drought & Heatwave
Increasing Frequency
Drought & Heat
⏰ June–September (esp. July–August)
Moderate stress → concentration; severe → ripening stalls/sunburn, yields –30–50%
  • Clay/old vines have advantage
  • Sand/young vines vulnerable
🛡 Irrigation · cover crops · canopy management · drought-resistant rootstock
⚠️ By 2050, could occur every 2–3 years
slides.7.title: Climate Risks (Part 2): Secondary and Compound Threats
slides.7.content:
🌧️ Excessive Rainfall
High
Excessive Rainfall
⏰ Flowering · Ripening · Harvest
  • Poor pollination → fruit drop (flowering)
  • Dilution of concentration (ripening)
  • Botrytis outbreak (harvest)
🛡 Drainage · canopy ventilation · harvest timing decisions
🦠 Disease Outbreaks
Medium–High
Disease Outbreaks
Three Major Typical Diseases
  • Downy mildew: 20–25°C warm and humid
  • Powdery mildew: 25–28°C warm and dry
  • Botrytis cinerea: humid conditions at ripening
🛡 Predictive models · ventilation · precise spray timing
⚠️ Organic farming restricts copper use; greater pressure in wet years
💨 Storms & Strong Winds
Medium
Storms & Wind
⏰ Year-round, primarily in autumn
  • Branch breakage · leaf tearing
  • Bunch drop
  • Disease risk ↑ after storm (via wounds)
🛡 Reinforce stakes · choose sheltered parcels · train vines appropriately · insurance
slides.8.title: Knowledge Check: Risk Mechanisms
slides.8.question: Why might spring frost risk actually increase in the context of a warming climate (as demonstrated by 2017)?
slides.8.options.1: Warmer winters cause vines to break bud earlier, but the possibility of cold air masses moving south in spring still exists, causing the vulnerable period to overlap with the frost period
slides.8.options.2: Climate change increases the frequency of polar cold air incursions
slides.8.options.3: Bordeaux is moving northward into a higher-latitude frost zone
slides.8.explanation: This is a counterintuitive but critically important climate change impact. Warmer winters cause vines to end dormancy earlier, with bud-break advanced by 10–14 days (e.g., from 20 April to 6 April). However, the possibility of cold air masses moving south in spring has not disappeared; it may even increase due to instability in the polar vortex caused by warming in the Arctic. This means that the vine's vulnerable period (from bud-break to leaf expansion) more easily overlaps with the high-risk frost period. The frost on 27–28 April 2017 is a classic case: early bud-break + sudden cold air = catastrophic losses. This proves that 'warming = fewer frosts' is incorrect, and new risk management strategies are needed.
slides.9.title: Integrated Risk Management Strategy Framework
slides.9.subtitle: A Systematic Approach from Prevention to Response
slides.10.title: Five-Pillar Framework for Risk Management
slides.10.content:
① Prevention
Reduce the probability or severity of risk occurrence
  • Parcel selection (slope/good drainage)
  • Variety and rootstock (late bud-break/drought-tolerant)
  • Infrastructure (drainage/frost protection/anti-hail nets)
⏳ Long-term investment (years to decades)
② Monitoring
Detect risks promptly to allow response time
  • Micro weather stations + satellite remote sensing
  • Soil moisture sensors
  • Disease prediction models
⚡ Warning 6–48 hours in advance
③ Response
Immediate action when risk occurs
  • Activate heaters/fans on frost nights
  • Accelerate harvest decisions ahead of rain
  • Rapid damage assessment after hail
💰 Requires rapid decision-making + adequate equipment reserves
④ Adaptation
Adjust long-term strategy based on risk experience
  • Variety conversion (heat- and drought-tolerant)
  • Adjust planting density/vine training
  • Geographic diversification (multiple appellations)
⚠️ Variety changes may affect AOC classification
⑤ Economic Hedging
Use financial instruments to reduce economic losses
  • Frost/hail/drought insurance (70–80% coverage)
  • Premium approx. 3–8% of annual revenue
  • Reserve fund + diversified income (e.g. tourism)
📌 Cannot compensate for quality losses and reputational damage
slides.11.title: Risk Management Strategies for Estates of Different Scales
slides.11.content:
Scale determines resources, resources determine strategy — risk management capability is a core competitive advantage in the modern wine industry
🌱 Small Estates
< 5 ha · Limited resources
✅ Available Strategies
  • Careful parcel selection
  • Meticulous manual management
  • Focus on disease prevention
  • Flexibility in harvest timing
  • Neighbour cooperation network
Expensive equipment unaffordable; high premiums; high risk of survival crisis in disaster years
🏡 Medium-sized Estates
5–30 ha · Medium resources
✅ Available Strategies
  • Invest in frost protection for core parcels
  • Install weather station
  • Agricultural insurance
  • Optical sorting table
  • Moderate financial reserves
Must allocate limited resources across multiple risks; geographic diversification difficult
🏰 Large Groups
> 30 ha · Ample resources
✅ Available Strategies
  • Comprehensive risk management system
  • Advanced monitoring technology
  • Geographic diversification across multiple appellations
  • R&D investment
  • Comprehensive insurance coverage
Economies of scale + risk diversification → strong resilience
slides.12.title: Knowledge Check: Risk Management
slides.12.question: In the difficult vintage of 2013, top estates (such as Château Margaux) still produced high-quality wines, while many small and medium estates struggled. Which dimension of risk management does this primarily reflect?
slides.12.options.0: Preventive measures — having selected disease-resistant varieties in advance
slides.12.options.1: Response measures — rigorous grape selection, green harvesting, and meticulous winemaking
slides.12.options.2: Economic hedging — having taken out adequate insurance
slides.12.options.3: Adaptive adjustment — having changed long-term planting strategy
slides.12.explanation: 2013 was a typical difficult vintage: rainy, high disease pressure, and insufficient ripeness. The key to top estates producing high-quality wines lay in 'response measures': rigorous green harvesting during the vineyard phase to remove poor-quality bunches; extremely strict grape selection at harvest, keeping only the healthiest grapes; using optical sorting tables to remove any damaged or underripe berries; and meticulous control during winemaking. These measures require large amounts of labour, advanced equipment, and the winemaker's professional judgement. Small and medium estates with limited resources found it difficult to exercise such strict selection, and quality gaps were enormous. This proves that in difficult vintages, the winemaker's skill and resource investment matter more than ever.

slides.14.subtitle: Extreme Vintages and Climate Risk Management
slides.14.summary: You have gained an in-depth understanding of the causes, impacts, and legacies of 10 key extreme vintages in Bordeaux history (1956, 1991, 2003, 2013, 2017–2022), developed a systematic understanding of the mechanisms and damage patterns of 6 major climate risk types, and mastered the 5 strategic dimensions of estate risk management. This knowledge will help you understand the root causes of vintage differences, evaluate the investment value of wines, and gain a deep appreciation of the challenges and opportunities facing the wine industry under climate change.
